title: Implicit Safety Alignment from Crowd Preferences
claim: Naive preference-learned rewards separate safe from unsafe behavior but systematically over-reward majority-preferred behavior over minority-preferred behavior.
layout: 2 side-by-side scatter-line panels, labeled (a)/(b), dashed vertical preference markers
description: Two side-by-side plots show predicted reward (y-axis) against velocity (x-axis) for two environments: Run (a) and HalfCheetah-vel (b). Each panel has faint scatter points of individual samples, green for safe and red for unsafe, with bold smoothed lines overlaid in the same colors. Vertical dashed lines mark preferences: blue for the majority preference and orange for the minority preference. In Run, the green safe curve sits high and declines gently from the blue line toward the orange line, while the red unsafe curve stays low and jagged. In HalfCheetah-vel, the green safe region lies between the orange and blue lines with rewards near zero and a peak near the blue line, while red unsafe regions on both sides have lower rewards. A legend in panel (a) explains the colors. The eye goes first to the bold green and red lines.
caption: Predicted rewards on safe and unsafe samples under the imbalanced crowd-preference setting. Safe trajectories (green) receive higher rewards than unsafe ones (red), while trajectories aligned with the majority preference (blue) are over-rewarded compared to minority-preferred ones (yellow).
abstract: Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) can reveal implicit objectives such as safety considerations that go beyond task completion. In this work, we focus on the common safety criteria embedded in crowd preference datasets, where different users may express distinct preferences or objectives, yet follow similar safety principles. Our aim is to discover shared safety criteria from crowd preferences and then transfer them to downstream RL tasks to regularize agent behavior and enforce safety. We first show that direct reward combination-optimizing a preference-learned reward model together with downstream task rewards-has inherent limitations. Motivated by this, we propose Safe Crowd Preference-based RL, a hierarchical framework that extracts safety-aligned skills from crowd preferences and composes them via a high-level policy to safely solve downstream tasks. Experiments across safe RL environments and a preliminary LLM-style task with diverse user goals and shared safety constraints demonstrate that our approach substantially lowers safety costs without access to explicit safety rewards, while achieving task performance comparable to oracle methods trained with ground-truth safety signals.
